qs.q: Which of the following forms of malaria transmission can occur congenitally across the placenta?
qs.e: Vertical transmission occurs across the placenta from mother to fetus, alongside blood transfusion transmission. Vector-borne transmission involves mosquito bites.

qs.q: If an identical twin develops ALL during the first year of life and they shared a monochorionic placenta, what is the approximate risk that the second twin will also develop ALL?
qs.e: The risk to the second twin is greater than 70% if ALL is diagnosed in the first twin during the first year of life and they shared a monochorionic placenta. Twins diagnosed later have significantly lower relative risks.

qs.q: At what gestational age do maternal immunoglobulins, such as IgG, begin to be transferred to the fetus via the placenta?
qs.e: The transfer of maternal immunoglobulins to the fetus begins at 32-34 weeks' gestation. Earlier gestational ages lack this full placental barrier and immunological transfer capacity.

qs.q: In pre-eclampsia, an ischemic placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors into the maternal circulation. Which factor is increased to cause endothelial dysfunction?
qs.e: The ischemic placenta in pre-eclampsia releases increased amounts of sFlt-1 (a VEGF/PlGF antagonist) while decreasing PlGF levels. This imbalance causes widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction and vasospasm.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The placenta is a temporary organ that connects the developing fetus to the uterine wall. It facilitates nutrient uptake, waste elimination, and gas exchange via the mother's blood supply. It also produces hormones essential for pregnancy maintenance.

sections.p: The placenta is a vital, transient organ that develops during pregnancy. It serves as the interface between the mother and the fetus, enabling the exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products. It also plays a crucial endocrine role.
b: Expelled after the fetus is born.
Essential for fetal survival and growth.
Implantation site is usually fundal or high lateral.
Fetal surface is smooth and shiny.
Maternal surface is rough and lobulated.

sections.p: The placenta is intimately related to the decidua basalis of the uterine wall, forming the maternal side. The fetal side is covered by the amnion and chorion, which also form the umbilical cord. The amniotic fluid surrounds the fetus and the fetal surface of the placenta.
b: Connected to fetus via umbilical cord.

sections.p: The placenta receives maternal blood from the uterine arteries and returns it via the uterine veins. Fetal blood circulates within the placental villi, supplied by the umbilical arteries and drained by the umbilical vein. This dual circulation allows for efficient exchange.

The placenta itself lacks intrinsic nerve supply. Its functions are regulated by maternal and fetal hormonal and vascular mechanisms. Autonomic nerves in the uterine wall influence blood flow to the placenta.
b: Uterine nerves affect placental blood flow.

sections.p: The placenta performs several critical functions: gas exchange (oxygen and carbon dioxide), nutrient transfer (glucose, amino acids, fats, vitamins, minerals), waste removal (urea, bilirubin), antibody transfer (passive immunity), and hormone production (progesterone, estrogen, hCG) to maintain pregnancy.

Abnormalities in placental location or function can lead to significant complications. Placenta previa, where the placenta covers the cervix, necessitates Cesarean delivery. Placental abruption, the premature separation from the uterine wall, causes maternal hemorrhage and fetal distress. Poor placental function can result in fetal growth restriction.

When examining the placenta after delivery, note its size, shape, and completeness. Ensure no fragments are retained in the uterus, which can cause postpartum hemorrhage or infection. The umbilical cord should have three vessels (two arteries, one vein).

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of fetal distress (decreased fetal movements).

faq.q: What is the main role of the placenta?
faq.a: To provide oxygen and nutrients to the fetus and remove waste products.
A condition where the placenta partially or completely covers the cervix, often leading to bleeding.

faq.q: Can the placenta cause problems after birth?
faq.a: Yes, retained placental fragments can cause bleeding or infection.
